newsitem.title: USA: Dancer Juliet Prowse dead at age 59.
newsitem.headline: Dancer Juliet Prowse dead at age 59.

text.p: Juliet Prowse, who danced her way to stardom in the 1960s with a combination of grace, charm and long legs, died on Saturday after a battle against pancreatic cancer. She was 59 years old.
Prowse, whose career spanned movies, television, stage musicals and nightclubs, died at her Los Angeles home with her son, Seth McCook, at her bedside, said publicist Marcia Groff.

Prowse was diagnosed with cancer in 1994 but it was reportedly in remission last year and she was well enough to perform during a 10-week summer run of "Sugar Babies" at a Las Vegas nightclub. But her condition began deteriorating earlier this year.

Trained as a ballerina while growing up in South Africa, Prowse was lured to Hollywood and shot to stardom in 1960 with major roles in two hit movie musicals -- "Can-Can," opposite Frank Sinatra, and "G.I. Blues," opposite Elvis Presley.
At the time the tabloids were filled with reports of her romances with her two leading men. Prowse broke off an engagement to Sinatra in 1962 after only a few weeks.
But it was an encounter with Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev that first brought her international exposure.

During a 1959 visit to the movie set while "Can-Can" was being filmed, Khrushchev watched the then-unknown Prowse and others rehearsing their steps. The next day he denounced the dance as immoral. Prowse's photo was soon splashed across newspapers worldwide.
Prowse was born in Bombay, India, to South African parents and was educated in South Africa where she attended the Royal Academy of Dance.
She was pursuing a career as a dancer in European nightclubs when famed Hollywood choreographer Hermes Pan spotted her and gave her a role in "Can-Can."
She was an instant success in acting and dancing parts and others films followed, including "The Fiercest Heart," "The Right Approach" and "Second Time Around."
Her movie career was relatively short, effectively ending in 1966 with "Run for Your Wife." Her other movies included "An American Wife," "Dingaka" and "Who Killed Teddy Bear?", all released in 1965.
But she remained a lasting success in television specials, threatrical productions and nightclub acts.

She appeared in a London production of "Kismet" and toured the United States in productions of "Sweet Charity," "Irma La Douce," "On A Clear Day You Can See Forever," "Mame," "The Pajama Game" and "Follies."
In 1965 Prowse starred in a TV series entitled "Mona McCluskey" -- about a movie star married to an Air Force sergeant -- but it was cancelled after just one season.
In 1987 Prowse was injured when she was attacked by a trained leopard during rehearsal for a TV special called "Circus of the Stars."

She received five stitches and, saying the animal was just "overly affectionate," returned to complete filming. But two months later while preparing for a "Tonight Show" TV appearance to promote "Circus of the Stars" she was mauled again by the same leopard and needed dozens of stitches for wounds to her jaw, ear and neck.
Prowse, who became a U.S. citizen in 1980, is survived by her son, Seth McCook, her mother and her brother.
